content: Herpangina, also known as vesicular stomatitis or acute lymphonodular pharyngitis, is a self-limiting infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by enteroviruses. The most commonly implicated pathogens are serotypes of coxsackie A virus. Outbreaks of herpangina are frequently observed during the summer months, predominantly affecting children. The disease typically begins with a sudden onset of fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), and the appearance of enanthem (oral lesions). Diagnosis is primarily clinical, and the condition usually resolves within one week without long-term complications. The term herpangina was first introduced by Zahorsky, who provided a detailed clinical description of the disease in 1920. The coxsackie virus, a major causative agent, was first isolated and described in 1948 by Dalldorf and Sickles. Herpangina is caused by enteroviruses, with the majority of cases attributed to coxsackie A viruses, particularly serotypes A1, A2, A6, A8, A10, A16, and A22. Other enteroviruses, such as certain coxsackie B virus serotypes, echoviruses, and enterovirus 71, can also be responsible. The primary mode of transmission for enteroviruses is the fecal-oral route. However, the virus can also spread through contact with virus-contaminated oral secretions, vesicular fluid, contaminated surfaces or objects (fomites), and respiratory droplets. After ingestion, the virus replicates in the lymphoid tissues of the oropharyngeal cavity and Peyer’s patches in the small intestine. Dissemination to the reticuloendothelial system and other tissues, such as the skin and mucous membranes, coincides with the onset of clinical symptoms. Several risk factors are associated with herpangina, including attendance at daycare or kindergarten, contact with infected individuals, residence in rural areas, overcrowding, poor hygiene, and low socioeconomic status. Differential diagnoses for herpangina include other conditions that present with oral pain and blistering, such as herpetic gingivostomatitis (caused by herpes simplex virus), bacterial pharyngitis, tonsillitis, aphthous stomatitis, and hand-foot-mouth disease. Herpetic gingivostomatitis, for example, typically affects the anterior oral cavity, including the inner lips, buccal mucosa, and tongue, and may involve gingivitis and cervical lymphadenitis, which are not features of herpangina. The incidence of herpangina shows seasonal variation, with a peak during the summer. It predominantly affects children aged 3 to 10 years, though adolescents and young adults may occasionally be affected. There is no known sex predilection. Herpangina is a self-limiting condition, and complications such as meningitis are rare. The prognosis is excellent, with complete resolution typically occurring within one week. The clinical history of herpangina often includes sudden fever, sore throat, and dysphagia, which may precede the appearance of enanthem by several hours to 24 hours. Other symptoms may include vomiting, abdominal pain, myalgia, and headache. Pharyngeal lesions are characteristic, but most patients do not appear severely ill. On physical examination, the throat may show erythema and mild tonsillar exudate. The hallmark enanthem consists of punctate macules that evolve over 24 hours into 2-4 mm erythematous papules, which then vesiculate and centrally ulcerate. These lesions are typically few in number and evolve rapidly. They are most commonly observed on the soft palate and uvula but may also appear on the tonsils, posterior pharyngeal wall, and buccal mucosa. The diagnosis of herpangina is clinical. In uncertain cases, pharyngeal viral and bacterial cultures can help exclude herpes simplex virus infection and streptococcal pharyngitis. Approximately one week after infection, type-specific antibodies appear in the blood, with peak titers occurring at three weeks. Treatment for herpangina is symptomatic, as the infection is self-limiting. Management includes saline gargles, analgesic throat lozenges, and adequate oral fluid intake for sore throat relief. Analgesic and antipyretic medications may be used as needed. Antiviral and antibacterial medications are generally unnecessary, as symptoms resolve within one week. Prevention of herpangina involves infection control measures, such as maintaining good personal hygiene (e.g., handwashing), cleaning and disinfecting surfaces and objects, and quarantining infected children to prevent the spread of the virus.
